newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Oil refiners see threat to margins from gasoline.
newsitem.headline: Oil refiners see threat to margins from gasoline.

text.p: Refining margins are at satisfactory levels but static gasoline prices are raising concerns that margins have already peaked, European oil refinery economists said this week.

"Complex margins have held above $2 (a barrel). It's acceptable. Everyone should be happy, although it doesn't necessarily pay for all the investment made at the refinery," said an economist at one European refinery.
Gasoline has been the key market support with the United States drawing in 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes from Northwest Europe in the second half of April.
"Until last week, the gasoline-to-crude (price) ratio was well above five year values," one economist said.

Margins improved even further in April as demand from Asia propped up gas oil prices, naphtha provided some support at the start of the month and and crude prices made little recovery from their early year slide.
Few expect any further support from gas oil, naphtha can have only a limited effect on overall margins, but a number of refinery economists believe crude can slip further.
"In the mid-term, through summer, we expect crude to fall even further. There really isn't much bullish news around," said one.
The main concern, therefore, is gasoline which traditionally drives the market at through the spring and into summer months.
The spread between unleaded premium barges fob ARA and dated Brent has, however, softened from an end of March peak in excess of $6 a barrel to just over $5.
Low gasoline stock levels in the dominant United States market should be bullish, but have not urged prices higher in the last month.
"The U.S. just hasn't really taken off," a trader said.
Nor has economic growth had a large knock-on effect. In
the first three months of the year, U.S. gross domestic product grew at an annual rate of 5.6 percent, its largest gain since the fourth quarter of 1987.
"It just doesn't seem to have translated into gasoline use and they should be buying more cars," an economist said.

A forecast in April by the Energy Information Agency that gasoline demand is expected to rise by 1.8 percent to a record 8.14 million barrels per day (bpd) this summer has failed to inspire confidence for the ensuing months.
"We're moving out of peak maintenance period and a lot of product is going to come available," a European trader said.
The consensus view therefore is that, with no sign of increased life from U.S. drivers yet, there is little prospect of margins recovering to their early April levels.
"The margins are unlikely to crumble, but there really is not a lot of upward potential," said one economist.
"We can't see the April margins lasting: and there is no strong demand in Europe at all," said another.
BP said on Tuesday that average refinery margins in Europe fell 80 cents to $1.6 a barrel in the first quarter this year from the fourth quarter 1996.
This is also below the average $2 a barrel in the first quarter 1996.
-- Philip Blenkinsop, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5004
